title: Toy Story 5 Lands in India This Friday. Its Villain Is the Screen in Your Child's Hand.
excerpt: Pixar's $3 billion franchise returns June 19 in English and Hindi, facing down a tablet, a China controversy, and a Bollywood showdown — with $4 billion on the line.
body:
When *Toy Story 5* opens in Indian cinemas this Friday — June 19, in both English and Hindi — it arrives carrying a weight no animated sequel should have to bear. It needs to do more than make children laugh. It needs to justify why the toys came back at all, seven years after *Toy Story 4* delivered what most critics called a perfect ending. And for the millions of Indian diaspora parents who grew up with Woody and Buzz, this fifth chapter lands on an unexpectedly personal nerve: the screen in your child's hand.

## The Premise Cuts Close to Home

The setup is almost uncomfortably relevant. Bonnie, the little girl who inherited Andy's toys at the end of the third film, has become attached to a tablet — a sentient device named **Lilypad**, voiced by Greta Lee. As technology threatens to make traditional playtime obsolete, Woody (**Tom Hanks**), Buzz (**Tim Allen**), Jessie (**Joan Cusack**) and the rest of the gang must prove they still matter in a world where a glowing rectangle commands a child's full attention.

If that plot makes you glance guiltily at your own kid scrolling Cocomelon at the dinner table, that's precisely the point. Director **Andrew Stanton** — the man behind *Finding Nemo* and *WALL-E*, the latter itself a meditation on technology and disconnection — has built the entire film around the anxiety that defines modern parenting across every culture. For NRI families navigating the same screen-time battles in Sunnyvale and Edison as their counterparts in Mumbai, *Toy Story 5* isn't escapism. It's a mirror.

## The Numbers Tell a Story of Their Own

The commercial stakes are enormous. The first four *Toy Story* films have collectively grossed **$3.03 billion** worldwide. *Toy Story 5* needs to earn roughly **$967 million** to push the franchise past the historic **$4 billion** mark — a milestone almost no film series ever reaches. Early tracking points to a domestic opening weekend of **$150 million to $175 million**, which would give it a strong head start toward that target.

It helps that *Toy Story* may be the most beloved animated franchise on the planet. The original films hold near-perfect critical scores — 100%, 100%, 98% and 97% on Rotten Tomatoes — a consistency that no other major franchise can claim. Pixar has stumbled with other sequels and prequels in recent years, but the toys have never once let audiences down.

## The Controversy Nobody Saw Coming

What almost derailed the entire release had nothing to do with the film itself. According to reporting by *Puck*, Pixar Chief Creative Officer **Pete Docter** was allegedly considering a meeting with the Dalai Lama — a gesture that reportedly prompted China and its distributors to warn Disney that *Toy Story 5* would be blocked from the region entirely.

The stakes there are staggering. China is one of the largest markets for Disney-Pixar films; *Zootopia 2* recently grossed over $500 million there, a record for an imported movie. Losing China would have gutted the film's path to $1 billion. Disney has not commented, but the release is going ahead in the region — a quiet reminder that even a children's movie about talking toys cannot fully escape the geopolitics of global box office.

## A Friday Showdown in India

In India, *Toy Story 5* doesn't get a clean runway. It opens the same day as **Cocktail 2**, the Shahid Kapoor–Kriti Sanon drama that earned an 'A' certificate from the CBFC — meaning the two films aren't even chasing the same audience. That's a gift for exhibitors: a family-friendly Hindi-dubbed Pixar tentpole and an adult Bollywood release sharing the same weekend, each pulling its own crowd.

For diaspora families, the Hindi dub matters more than it might seem. It means grandparents visiting from India, cousins who prefer Hindi, and younger kids being raised bilingual can all share the same theatre experience without anyone feeling left out. Pixar's decision to release simultaneously in English and Hindi across Indian cinemas is a recognition that the *Toy Story* audience here is genuinely multigenerational.

## Why It Matters

There's something fitting about *Toy Story* — a franchise that began in 1995, the year many NRI millennials were children themselves — returning now to wrestle with the very technology reshaping their own kids' childhoods. The toys have always been about the things we outgrow and the love that outlasts them. Thirty years on, the question the films ask has only sharpened: in a world of infinite screens, does anything analog still get to matter?

This Friday, Indian audiences will help answer that question with their wallets. And if the early tracking holds, Woody and Buzz may just ride a tablet-obsessed little girl all the way to a $4 billion legacy.
